html:
The Maritime Jade Road was a sea trade network in which green nephrite jade from Taiwan was carried to the Philippines, worked into ornaments, and traded around the South China Sea. It lasted from roughly 2000 BCE to 1000 CE, one of the longest lived trade networks known from early times.

It grew with the spread of Austronesian peoples by boat from Taiwan south into the islands; see Austronesians reach the Philippines. Chemical tests trace much of the jade to a single source near Hualien in eastern Taiwan. At first finished tools and beads moved; later raw jade went to workshops in the Philippines, and finished pieces spread to Borneo, Vietnam and Thailand.

Its best known products are lingling-o, split ring earrings and pendants, some with two animal heads. The Sa Huynh culture of central Vietnam also made them. Archaeologists use the jade as a tracer for the movement of people and ideas across island Southeast Asia long before written records.
